definition: Archetypal analysis in statistics is an unsupervised learning method similar to cluster analysis and introduced by Adele Cutler and Leo Breiman in 1994.
details: Rather than "typical" observations (cluster centers), it seeks extremal points in the multidimensional data, the "archetypes". The archetypes are convex combinations of observations chosen so that observations can be approximated by convex combinations of the archetypes.

explainer.lead: Archetypal analysis summarizes a dataset through extreme points rather than average or typical ones. These archetypes can describe both the outer shape of the data and, through mixtures, the observations inside it.

tiers.eli5: Instead of finding the average person in a group, it finds the most extreme examples at the edges, and describes everyone as a blend of those.
tiers.practitioner: It seeks extremal points, the archetypes, which are convex combinations of observations chosen so observations can be approximated by convex combinations of the archetypes; a pitfall is that archetypes sit at the data's extremes, so they can be outliers rather than typical cases.
tiers.paperLevel: Archetypes are convex combinations of observations, chosen so that each observation is approximated by a convex combination of the archetypes; unlike cluster centers, they are extremal points of the multidimensional data.

explainer.example: Suppose the archetypes for three two-dimensional observations are (0,0), (10,0), and (0,10). An observation at (2,3) is exactly reconstructed with weights 0.5, 0.2, and 0.3: 0.5(0,0) + 0.2(10,0) + 0.3(0,10) = (2,3). The weights are nonnegative and sum to one.
explainer.intuition: Cluster analysis asks which typical points best represent groups; archetypal analysis asks which extreme points span the data. Each observation is then explained as a mixture of those extremes.
howItWorks: Represent candidate archetypes as convex combinations of the observations.
Represent each observation as a convex combination of the archetypes.
Choose the archetypes so these combinations approximate the observations well.
Use the resulting archetypes and mixture weights to summarize the data.
explainer.whyItMatters: It provides a summary based on the boundaries of the data while still expressing interior observations as interpretable mixtures. This complements summaries based only on central or typical observations.
misconceptions: Archetypes are not cluster centers: they represent extremes rather than typical observations.
An archetype need not be an original observation, because it can be a convex combination of several.

diagram.caption: Archetypes are built from observations, then mixed to approximate those observations.
